title: Federal Reserve Board announces final individual capital requirements for large banks, effective on October 1
summary: The Federal Reserve Board announced final individual capital requirements for large banks on August 29, 2025, effective October 1. The requirements include a minimum 4.5% common equity tier 1 capital floor, a stress capital buffer based on stress test results (minimum 2.5%), and possible capital surcharges for the largest systemic banks. The announcement represents a transitional period pending a proposed rule to average stress test results over two consecutive years to reduce year-over-year volatility.
key_points: Final individual capital requirements for large banks announced, effective October 1, 2025
Capital requirements include minimum 4.5% CET1 floor, stress capital buffer of at least 2.5%, and potential capital surcharge for largest/most complex banks
In April 2025, the Board proposed a rule to average stress test results over two consecutive years to reduce volatility; if finalized, this year's results will be averaged with 2024 results
Banks below total capital requirements face automatic restrictions on capital distributions and discretionary bonus payments
Morgan Stanley's stress capital buffer requirement is deferred pending reconsideration request; final requirement expected by September 30, 2025
Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman described the announcement as representing a period of transition toward reduced volatility and increased transparency
why_it_matters: Bank capital requirements directly affect how large banks allocate capital, manage risk, and distribute profits. The stress capital buffer framework influences the amount of capital banks must hold against potential losses in adverse scenarios, which affects their ability to pay dividends and execute buybacks. The pending averaging rule could significantly affect capital requirement calculations going forward.
market_structure_context: This announcement establishes the capital framework for large US banks based on the 2025 stress test cycle. The stress capital buffer requirement mechanism is a key component of how the Fed ensures banks maintain sufficient capital to absorb losses in severe recessions. The pending rule to average two years of stress test results would reduce the year-over-year volatility banks face in their capital requirements, potentially allowing more stable capital planning.
